theme: The altar, the court, the priestly garments
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 27:1-28:43. Yesterday took you inside the tent. Today takes you to the courtyard and to the clothes of the priests. As you read the description of the altar and the garments, ask what each one says about how a sinner can come near to God.
settingTheScene: The instructions for the tabernacle continue. Chapter 27 describes the bronze altar of burnt offering, which stands at the entrance, and the surrounding courtyard. Chapter 28 turns from the building to the people who will serve in it. Aaron and his sons are chosen as priests, and God gives detailed instructions for their garments. These are not ordinary clothes. They are “for glory and for beauty” (28:2), and each piece carries meaning.
observation: The altar of burnt offering is made of acacia wood covered with bronze, with horns at its four corners (27:1-8).
The courtyard is enclosed by linen curtains, so that the people see the altar before they see the tent (27:9-19).
The lamp is to burn “from evening to morning before the LORD” as a perpetual statute (27:20-21).
Aaron and his sons are “brought near” from among the people of Israel to serve as priests (28:1).
The high priest wears an ephod with two onyx stones, each engraved with the names of six tribes (28:9-12).
The breastpiece has twelve stones with the names of the twelve tribes, and Aaron is to bear them “on his heart” when he enters the Holy Place (28:15-21, 29).
On the turban is a plate of pure gold engraved “Holy to the LORD” (28:36).
Aaron bears “any guilt from the holy things that the people of Israel consecrate” (28:38).
interpretation:
The order of the building teaches something. To approach the tabernacle, a worshiper had to pass through the gate and meet the bronze altar first. Before anyone could draw near to God, a sacrifice had to be made. The altar stood directly in the way. There was no path around it. The first lesson of the tabernacle is that sinners come to God by way of a substitute.

The second lesson is the role of the priest. Notice that Aaron is “brought near” (28:1), which means he was chosen, not self-appointed. No one can walk into God’s presence on his own. A mediator is needed, and God provides one. Every piece of the priest’s clothing speaks of his task. The ephod and breastpiece carry the names of the twelve tribes, on his shoulders and on his heart. He represents the people before God, with their weight on his shoulders and their names near his heart.

The gold plate on the turban says “Holy to the LORD.” It is a remarkable detail. The priest is himself a sinner, and the people’s offerings are imperfect. Yet verse 38 says that Aaron bears “any guilt” connected with their gifts. The plate on his forehead is a sign that even the best worship of sinners needs to be covered. This is humbling. Even our worship is not good enough without a mediator.

Finally, notice the “glory and beauty” of the clothing. The gold, blue, purple, and scarlet threads are the same colors as the tabernacle curtains. The priest is dressed like the building. This shows that the priest belongs to the sanctuary. It also shows that God’s holiness is beautiful and not only fearsome. He is not a harsh master but a God of glory, and he wants his people to see it.
connection: Hebrews tells you that Jesus is the great high priest who has passed through the heavens (Hebrews 4:14), who “always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25). Unlike Aaron, he has no sin of his own to cover (Hebrews 7:27). Peter says that all believers are now “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9). The altar finds its fulfillment at the cross, where Jesus offered himself once for all (Hebrews 10:10).
application:
Praise God for your mediator. Picture Jesus carrying your name on his shoulders and over his heart, as Aaron did for Israel.

If you tend to think that your prayers and worship need to be perfect before God will receive them, remember the gold plate. He receives them because of the priest, not because of you.

Ask God to help you serve others as a priest, by praying for them and bringing their needs before him.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for carrying you on his shoulders and on his heart.
Ask him to teach you to pray for others as he prays for you.
Thank him that your worship is received because of him.
